title: Ἔλαφος καὶ ἄμπελος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 103. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔλαφος κυνηγοὺς φεύγουσα ὑπ᾽ ἀμπέλῳ ἐκρύβη.
sentences.tr: Elaphos kynēgous pheugousa hyp’ ampelōi ekrybē.
sentences.l: A deer, fleeing hunters, hid under a vine.
sentences.n: ἔλαφος is feminine here (φεύγουσα, and the participles that follow), so the deer is a doe throughout. φεύγω with a bare accusative is 'flee from', no preposition needed.

sentences.t: Παρελθόντων δ᾽ ὀλίγον ἐκείνων, ἡ ἔλαφος τελέως ἤδη λαθεῖν δόξασα, τῶν τῆς ἀμπέλου φύλλων ἐσθίειν ἤρξατο.
sentences.tr: Parelthontōn d’ oligon ekeinōn, hē elaphos teleōs ēdē lathein doxasa, tōn tēs ampelou phyllōn esthiein ērxato.
sentences.l: And they having passed by a little, the deer, thinking she had by now escaped notice entirely, began to eat the leaves of the vine.
sentences.i: When they had gone a little way past, the deer, sure by now that she was altogether unseen, began to eat the vine's leaves.
sentences.n: Παρελθόντων … ἐκείνων is a genitive absolute — a noun and participle in the genitive, standing free of the main sentence's grammar, giving the circumstance. It is the fables' commonest way of moving time along, and there is another in the next sentence. λανθάνω is 'escape notice', the verb for doing anything unobserved; δόξασα λαθεῖν is 'having supposed that she had got away unseen'.

sentences.t: Τούτων δὲ σειομένων, οἱ κυνηγοὶ ἐπιστραφέντες καί, ὅπερ ἦν ἀληθές, νομίσαντες τῶν ζῴων ὑπὸ τοῖς φύλλοις τι κρύπτεσθαι, βέλεσιν ἀνεῖλον τὴν ἔλαφον.
sentences.tr: Toutōn de seiomenōn, hoi kynēgoi epistraphentes kai, hoper ēn alēthes, nomisantes tōn zōiōn hypo tois phyllois ti kryptesthai, belesin aneilon tēn elaphon.
sentences.l: And these being shaken, the hunters, having turned round and having supposed — which was in fact true — that one of the beasts was hiding under the leaves, killed the deer with their darts.
sentences.i: As the leaves shook, the hunters turned round and supposed, as was in fact the case, that one of the beasts lay hidden under the foliage, and brought the deer down with their darts.
sentences.n: A second genitive absolute (Τούτων … σειομένων) hard on the first. ὅπερ ἦν ἀληθές is the narrator stepping in for four words to say that the guess happened to be right — the hunters reason from the shaking leaves and are not wrong. τῶν ζῴων … τι is partitive, 'some one of the animals'.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ θνῄσκουσα τοιαῦτ᾽ ἔλεγε· « Δίκαια πέπονθα· οὐ γὰρ ἔδει τὴν σώσασάν με λυμαίνεσθαι. »
sentences.tr: Hē de thnēiskousa toiaut’ elege· « Dikaia pepontha· ou gar edei tēn sōsasan me lymainesthai. »
sentences.l: And she, dying, said such things as these: « I have suffered just things; for I ought not to have outraged the one who saved me. »
sentences.i: And as she died she said: « I have got what I deserved; I should never have harmed the one who saved me. »
sentences.n: Δίκαια πέπονθα is an idiom: 'I have suffered just things', that is, I have got exactly what I deserved. ἔδει with the infinitive states an obligation that was not met — 'I ought not to have', with the failure built into the past tense. τὴν σώσασαν is feminine because ἡ ἄμπελος is, and the feminine participle keeps the vine a person to the last word.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ ἀδικοῦντες τοὺς εὐεργέτας ὑπὸ θεοῦ κολάζονται.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti hoi adikountes tous euergetas hypo theou kolazontai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that those who wrong their benefactors are punished by god.
sentences.n: ὑπὸ θεοῦ has no article: not Zeus, not a named Olympian, but the divine as such — the impersonal justice these morals appeal to.
